rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

evidence_timeline.summary: Core collapse supernovae (CCSNe) are invoked as major dust producers in the early Universe, yet the amount of dust they form, the timescale over which it grows, and the physical conditions that regulate the yield remain uncertain. We present a detailed JWST/MIRI mid-infrared (MIR) imaging census of 11 nearby Type IIP CCSNe spanning $\sim$1-7 yr after explosion, investigating dust emission across the different phases of their evolution. The spectral energy distributions show a coherent evolution from hot ($\sim$1500 K), 5-8 $μ$m emission at $\sim$400 d to prominent 10 and 18 $μ$m emission features at later epochs ($\sim$600-2500 d). The cool dust temperatures range from $\sim120$ to $250$ K and dust masses from $\sim10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2} M_{\odot}$. The current sample shows no statistically significant correlation between measured dust mass and peak luminosity, plateau duration, or explosion energy. SNe with early high ionization features, indicative of confined CSM, are often among the dust-rich objects in the sample. The measured 1-7 yr dust yields are insufficient to account for dust in typical $z > 6$ galaxies, but support a role for CCSNe as producers of seed dust for subsequent grain growth.

evidence_timeline.summary: The Hubble Advanced Spectral Products (HASP) program is designed to robustly coadd Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS) and Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) spectra within the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST) in an automated fashion such that coadds are available for new data or archival data with updated calibrations. For each target within a visit or program, HASP employs a meticulous multi-stage filtering process to ensure data quality and creates coadded products for all central wavelengths (CENWAVEs) within specific gratings, as well as combined products using different gratings and instruments. The project also emphasizes making the code accessible to the user community for custom coaddition. As calibrations improve and new data are added to the archive, HASP products are re-created automatically so that they represent the best reduction of a given visit or program. Automated coadditions like those achieved by HASP can significantly enhance the combination of different CENWAVES, increase signal-to-noise ratios, and increase wavelength coverage. These properties make HASP a vital resource for astronomers using archival spectroscopic data from HST.
